steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a distributed computing paper giving a sufficient epistemic condition for solving stabilizing agreement. Open with a playful variant of a classic puzzle, relate stabilizing agreement to consensus and similar problems, and explain the epistemic logic background and our goal.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
We introduce the stabilizing agreement problem with a twist on a famous puzzle. The two kingdoms of Aldinga and Beluga have decided to join their powers and merge their kingdoms, but they have not agreed under which name they will continue to write history. The kingdoms are on two hills with a valley between them, and unfortunately a hungry dragon lives in that valley.

Luckily the dragon is getting slow and only ever eats at most one of the two messengers going between the two kingdoms (sometimes it catches neither). Neither Aldinga nor Beluga is in a rush to agree on one of the names, but they both know they should eventually start using the same name, because their heroic deeds are only impressive enough to leave a mark in the history books if they appear under the same name forever.

The situation of Aldinga and Beluga comes from the two generals problem, and it is not surprising that the two kingdoms also cannot solve consensus. But interestingly, prior work showed that stabilizing agreement is possible in this communication setting, which shows that stabilizing agreement is a proper weakening of the terminating consensus problem. Aldinga and Beluga can also solve the non-byzantine version of the firing-rebels problem, which is a non-simultaneous firing version of the firing squad, if they choose to fire on the dragon. This suggests a hierarchy of the three problems: consensus is the strongest and implies stabilizing agreement and the firing rebels, stabilizing agreement implies firing rebels, and firing rebels is the weakest of the three. This conjecture is supported by the fact that the sufficient knowledge for stabilizing agreement shown in this paper implies the sufficient knowledge for firing rebels, and by stabilizing agreement being a non-terminating relaxation of consensus.

- Formal setting / epistemic logic
  - distributed system: processes (agents) communicate and coordinate to solve problems like consensus (cite)
  - temporal epistemic logic very successful for distributed systems (cite)
  - Knowledge of Precondition Principle, Moses (cite); happened-before relation, Lamport (cite)
  - common knowledge operator (everybody knows that everybody knows etc.) ~ perfect coordination, needed for consensus (cite)
  - fault-tolerant Firing Rebels needs eventual common epistemic attitude (cite)
- Stabilizing vs consensus

  - agent may pick a value, later discover another value more likely common
  - agents ever-guessing: no guarantee of knowing when all values obtained

  - provide sufficient condition for solving stabilizing agreement

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
We introduce the stabilizing agreement problem with a twist on a famous puzzle. The two kingdoms of Aldinga and Beluga have decided to join their powers and merge their kingdoms, but they have not agreed under which name they will continue to write history. The kingdoms are on two hills with a valley between them, and unfortunately a hungry dragon lives in that valley.

Luckily the dragon is getting slow and only ever eats at most one of the two messengers going between the two kingdoms (sometimes it catches neither). Neither Aldinga nor Beluga is in a rush to agree on one of the names, but they both know they should eventually start using the same name, because their heroic deeds are only impressive enough to leave a mark in the history books if they appear under the same name forever.

The situation of Aldinga and Beluga comes from the two generals problem, and it is not surprising that the two kingdoms also cannot solve consensus. But interestingly, prior work showed that stabilizing agreement is possible in this communication setting, which shows that stabilizing agreement is a proper weakening of the terminating consensus problem. Aldinga and Beluga can also solve the non-byzantine version of the firing-rebels problem, which is a non-simultaneous firing version of the firing squad, if they choose to fire on the dragon. This suggests a hierarchy of the three problems: consensus is the strongest and implies stabilizing agreement and the firing rebels, stabilizing agreement implies firing rebels, and firing rebels is the weakest of the three. This conjecture is supported by the fact that the sufficient knowledge for stabilizing agreement shown in this paper implies the sufficient knowledge for firing rebels, and by stabilizing agreement being a non-terminating relaxation of consensus.

Formally, we look at a distributed system made of multiple processes, also called agents, that communicate and coordinate actions to solve some given problem, like consensus. Temporal epistemic logic has been a very successful framework for distributed systems, and it gave a number of crucial results, like the Knowledge of Precondition Principle formulated by Moses and the happened-before relation formulated by Lamport. Epistemic logic also showed that the common knowledge operator (everybody knows that everybody knows etc.) is closely related to perfect coordination, which is required in consensus. Maybe not surprisingly, even the fault-tolerant version of the Firing Rebels problem needs an eventual common epistemic attitude, as earlier work has shown.

Stabilizing problems relax standard consensus in one important way. In both the goal is for all agents to agree on a common value, but stabilizing agreement does not require the agents to terminate. So an agent can choose a value in some state of the system, assuming it is the correct one, and only later find out that another value is more likely to be the common value. This simple-looking twist keeps the agents guessing forever, since in general agents have no guarantee of knowing when they have obtained all values.

Stabilizing agreement has been getting more attention recently, but its epistemic formalization is still missing. The goal of this paper is to fill this gap by giving a sufficient condition for solving stabilizing agreement.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
We introduce the stabilizing agreement problem with a twist on a famous puzzle: the two kingdoms of Aldinga and Beluga have decided to combine their powers and merge their kingdoms, but have not agreed under which name they will continue to write history. The kingdoms reside on two hills separated by a valley, where unfortunately a hungry dragon lives.

Fortunately, the dragon is getting slow and only ever eats at most one of the two messengers between the two kingdoms (but sometimes catches neither). Neither Aldinga nor Beluga is in a rush to agree on either name, but both know that they should eventually start to use the same name, as their heroic deeds are only impressive enough to leave a mark in the history books if they appear under the same name forever.

The situation of Aldinga and Beluga is derived from the two generals problem [1], and not surprisingly the two kingdoms cannot solve consensus either. Interestingly, though, [2] showed that stabilizing agreement is indeed possible in this communication setting, highlighting that stabilizing agreement is a proper weakening of the terminating consensus problem. Aldinga and Beluga can also solve the non-byzantine version of the firing-rebels problem [3], itself a non-simultaneous firing version of the firing squad [4], should they choose to fire on the dragon. This hints at a hierarchy of the three problems: consensus, the strongest, implies stabilizing agreement and the firing rebels; stabilizing agreement implies firing rebels; and firing rebels is the weakest of the three. This conjecture is backed by the fact that the sufficient knowledge for stabilizing agreement shown in this paper implies the sufficient knowledge for firing rebels [3], and by stabilizing agreement being a non-terminating relaxation of consensus.

Formally, we consider a distributed system consisting of multiple processes, also known as agents, that communicate and coordinate actions in order to solve some given problem, such as consensus [5,6]. Temporal epistemic logic has proved to be an extremely successful framework for distributed systems [7], providing a number of crucial results such as the Knowledge of Precondition Principle formulated by Moses [8] and the happened-before relation formulated by Lamport [9]. Another important insight from epistemic logic is that the common knowledge operator (everybody knows that everybody knows etc.) is closely related to perfect coordination, which consensus requires [7]. Perhaps unsurprisingly, even the fault-tolerant version of the Firing Rebels problem requires an eventual common epistemic attitude, as shown in [3].

Stabilizing problems relax standard consensus in one crucial way: although the goal in both is for all agents to agree on a common value, stabilizing agreement does not require agents to terminate. This means that an agent can choose a value in a certain state of the system, supposing that it is the correct one, only to discover later that another value is more likely to be the common value. This deceptively simple twist keeps the agents ever-guessing, as agents in general have no guarantee of knowing when they have obtained all values.

While stabilizing agreement has recently received increasing attention [10,2], its epistemic formalization is still missing. This paper aims to fill this gap by providing a sufficient condition for solving stabilizing agreement.
